Uniform Title: Tattvaratnāvalī Author: Vimalaśiva Manuscript: NGMCP 1-1697-7/6 Reel Number: B 26/16

Description: *Tattvaratnāvalī* by Vimalaśiva, a South Indian Siddhāntin. This is a concise liturgical manual for the fundamental rites of Siddhānta Śaivism. The first chapter treats the regular daily rite (*nitya*), and the second treats the occasional rite (*naimittika*) performed on special festive occasions. The third chapter deals with the worship of the basic *Navanābhamaṇḍala* consisting of nine sections—eight surrounding a central one—each containing nine parts of the eighty-one parts (*pada*) of the *Vyomavyāpin* mantra. This is the standard mantra of Siddhānta Śaivism, beginning with an invocation of Sadāśiva as *Vyomavyāpin*, that is, "the one who pervades the sky" (fully written out on folio 10).
Notes: Revision 0: December 17, 2013 Publication Country: India Tattvaratnāvalī
1) Unclear.
2a) How can [the mantras] bestow the fruits of desire upon Śambhu, who is of a single form and devoid of ritual action (adhvara)?
The measurement of the mandala, complete with its doors and corners, consists of the central lotus-pedestal (*garbhapadma*), the surrounding space (*vyoma*), and twice that [space].
The petals, sub-petals,
and infinite filaments are described as being established according to their respective measurements within the pericarp.
What is the characteristic of the measurement of the other poisons and of the powders,
specifically for the purpose of nourishment, as well as for pacifying or killing?
O God, O Supreme Lord, when the lines are thick, very fine, or even deficient,
there will be both virtues and faults for that person, as well as their karma.

How is the *dollā* (swing) to be performed by the teachers for the practitioners and others? Established in one principle (*tattva*), there are indeed five principles belonging to the earth (*pārthiva*).
Which is the reality of the earth? It is that very [reality] of the waters, within the Lord.
What seed-syllables (*bīja*) are proclaimed for Fire and Wind in their own forms?
How do all the principles (*tattva*) [arise]?
O Śaṅkara, how does he become the source of the principles of strength and weakness?
It is taught that all have gone everywhere and all are cultivated by the Omniscient One. O Maheśvara, who are designated as impure, and who are designated as pure?
Having performed purification and ritual sipping (ācamana), one should worship the fire within the heart of the Goddess;
then, for the sake of accomplishing the stated purpose, one should tie a blade of darbha grass to the Goddess.
At the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), one should worship Agni with the Ajya-hṛdaya mantra;
one should offer three oblations, and thus perform the rite for a male child (puṃsavana).
One should cast the sparks of the armor-mantra into the fire from both the *vāmadeva* and *śiras* mantras;
and the form of the *sīmantonnayana* [rite] is performed with the *śikhā* mantra from the vicinity of the *śikhā*.

One should perform the visualization of the faces and limbs, as well as the rites of opening the mouth and expiation; having performed the birth-rite with the *jāta* and *varma* mantras, one should visualize the ten-armed Fire-god.

Having meditated on the five-faced mantra, one should kindle the fire with kusha grass; having meditated on the goddess’s golden bond that removes all afflictions, one should perform the ritual bathing.

One should sprinkle the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the Astra-mantra for immediate purification from birth-impurity (sūtaka). Then, having struck it with the Śastra-mantra and sprinkled it on the outside with the Varma-mantra;
With a blade, one should place the sacrificial grass (barhis) with its tips pointing toward the northeast;
there, one should arrange the enclosing sticks (paridhi) so that they are wider at the bottom and triangular in shape to ward off saliva.
Five fuel-sticks (samidh) soaked in clarified butter should be offered at the edge and the root;
one should worship Vidhi, Rudra, Hari, Veśa, and Paridhi in the east.
Having seated the world-protectors upon their seats, one should cause them to hear the command of Śiva:
"Having warded off the multitude of obstacles, you shall protect the child."
One should worship Vidhi, the presiding lord of the sacrifice, on the south with darbha grass and dried cow-dung;
one should worship Hari, the protector of the sacrifice, in the north with water in a vessel.
Then, taking the bracelet situated on the left hand of the Goddess,
he should hold the *sruva* and *sruk* ladles above and below [her] face, and [pour the offering] three times.

The preta [should be worshipped] with fire; one should sequentially place the three principles (tattvas) there using the root, middle, and tip of the darbha grass. Śakti is placed in the *sruc* ladle, and Śiva in the *sruva* spoon.
One should worship [the deity] by placing [the two vessels] with their necks encircled by a triple-strand cord upon one's own right [hand];
then, having performed the four purifications beginning with inspection, one should take this vessel.
Having meditated upon one's own body as that of Brahmā, one should rotate it three times above the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, having heated the fire— [and] having offered [oblations] with clarified butter, or with an elephant,
a horse, or a bull.
3a) If there is confusion regarding the pit, there will be confusion regarding the directions; if it lacks the proper measurement, there will be poverty;
if the cord is too long, there will be enmity with friends; and if it is devoid of a neck-ring, one will be hindered in speech.
There is failure and demonic enjoyment when [the line] is too short or too long;
there is exhaustion and an increase in disease when the girdle-line is too low or too high.

Apasmāra (epilepsy) occurs when [the breath] vibrates at the navel; bhagandara (fistula-in-ano) occurs at the navel; uccāṭana (expulsion) occurs when it is split; and when it is crowded with fissures, one becomes subject to censure.
Or one should offer oblations upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) with devotion, starting from the syllable *harānta*;
having gazed at that [ground] with the mantra beginning with *tattvadṛṣṭi*, one should then [proceed] with the *śara* mantra.
Having sprinkled [the site], struck it with the armor-mantra (tanutra), and thoroughly sprinkled it again while seated on kuśa grass;
having dug, extracted [the earth], filled [the pit], and leveled it with force.
Having cleansed and smeared [the site] with the perfected weapon-mantra,
having fashioned it into the form of the digits (kalā), and having encircled it with the three voids and the armor-mantra;
Having worshipped with the heart-mantra, one should draw three lines facing north using *kuśa* grass,
or one line facing east, or else there may be a reversal of these.
The performers of the rites, having offered oblations to Vṛtra,
draw the lines [of the altar] and perform the cleansing, drying, and baking in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) for the deities beginning with Brahmā.
Having made it adamantine with the Astra-mantra, one should fashion a four-way crossroads with Darbha grass using the Hṛdaya-mantra;
then, having placed a protective amulet of four Kuśa blades on the neck with the Varma-mantra.
Then, having offered with the heart-mantra, one should worship the goddess and the god with the heart-mantra;
having brought fire into a pure vessel, [one should offer] that which is devoid of the portion for carnivorous beings.

Having unified the fourfold purity beginning with gazing (vīkṣaṇa) and so forth, one should duly install the three fires— the digestive, the lunar, and the elemental— along with the consciousness (caitanya) of the syllable *hrūṃ*.

Having consecrated the fire with the Saṃhitā mantras and rendered it immortal, having protected it by encircling it with the Weapon and Armor mantras, and having worshipped it, one should circumambulate it clockwise.

Having rotated three times above the *kuṇḍa* while recollecting "the seed-syllable of Śiva," [one should fashion] the ploughshare (*potrā*) from the heart, facing oneself, measuring one-eighth [of the total].
3b) The proper measure for edible sugarcane is equal to a joint;
for boiled *kāśa* grass, it is half a mouthful; and for other grains, it is one full mouthful.

The measure for flowers, fruits, and leaves is their own weight; for a heap of rice, it is the measure of the grains; for parched grains, it is the measure of the vessel's capacity, or rather, the measure of its satisfaction.
The provincial governor, however, should offer oblations of half-a-piece of guggulu resin resembling bone, along with sesame, sugar-candy, kankaṇa, and so forth; such is the measure for a deer.
Sandalwood, camphor, saffron, musk, and the paste of *pakṣaka* should be offered as oblations; chickpeas and the like are suitable, and the creepers should be two finger-breadths in length.
Having thus completed the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite, one should perform the *pūrṇāhuti* at the end;
then, having offered betel leaf as a mouth-freshener along with the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) and hand-washing (*karodvarta*).
Having performed obeisance to their departure, having bowed and worshipped the Śaṃvaras,
and having withdrawn the weapons, one should place them in the heart while saying, "Forgive me."
Having prepared two mandalakas near the fire-pit,
one should take the first portion of all cooked food and offer it as an *antarvali* twice.
In the directions east, south, west, and north, [the deities are] Hara, Agni, Niti, and Anila;
and in the intermediate spaces, Bhīra resides between Indra and the Sky-dweller (Dhātṛ), and Pracetas between Indra and Vāyu.
The Rudras, the hosts of Mothers, Yakṣas, Grahas, Daityas, and Asuras; the Ṛkṣas, the Durāśayas, the Viśvas, the Ṛṣis, and the Kṣetrapālakas.
The mantra for the *tarpaṇa* is proclaimed as "sasvāhāḥ" followed by the *praṇava*.
Having offered the *bali* to Indra and the others, one should offer the *bali* to the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapati*) in the center.
In the second circle, one should offer the external bali as prescribed:
outcasts, those who have committed offenses, crows, dog-cookers, and those fallen from their caste.
Having arrived and accepted [the offering], while uttering "svāhā" externally,
one should give the bali, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then dismiss the bali-mantras.
Then, having offered it to Śiva along with water for the *argha* oblation,
one obtains the fruit of worship, fire-sacrifice (*homa*), and so forth, by means of the root mantra preceded by the heart-seed (*hṛdbīja*).
Having worshipped and praised Śiva, and having offered the arghya while [the deity] faces away,
one should then say "Forgive me," and subsequently withdraw the eternal [deity] from within the heart.
The most excellent of gurus should join [the image] into the pit of the pedestal with the Mūrti-mantra.
[The worship] is performed in an image, a friend, a bath, within the eyes,
in a painting, in a book, in a rosary of letters, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), and furthermore, within one's own self.
Then, having worshipped Caṇḍa and offered him the remains of the flowers (nirmālya) and other offerings, one should make this request:
"May whatever ritual act has been deficient or excessive be fulfilled."
Then, having been dismissed by Caṇḍanātha, one should purify one's being with cow dung;
thereafter, having worshipped a tawny cow (kapilā) and having offered her morsels of food.
Having worshipped the Vidyā according to the prescribed rite, one should worship the lotus feet of the Guru;
thereafter, the mantras of Śiva and the others are proclaimed in their proper sequence.

The root [mantra] consists of the *nāda* together with the *bindu*, conjoined with the sixth letter of the mantra; it is joined with the six long vowels and ends with the *jāti* [the *praṇava*], being the *gātra-śaṃvara*.
The Lord’s armor is joined with the short vowels in reverse order;
likewise, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *vaṣaṭ* are the four classes of suffixes.

When not explicitly stated, the Heart-mantra (hṛdaya) should be employed; all mantras beginning with the Fixed One (dhruva) end in "namaḥ" during worship, while they are declared to end in "svāhā" during the fire-oblation (homa).
Bowing deeply to Caṇḍāsana, likewise to Caṇḍamūrti,
and to Dhunicandeśvara with "Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā," [one attains] Dyusamvara.
One should apply the syllables joined with short and long vowels to the limbs of Brahmā;
one should fashion the faces beginning with "coḥ īśānāya hūṃ phaṭ" and so forth.

The heart-mantras and others, beginning with *caṇḍa* and ending with *huṃ phaṭ*, follow in sequence; then the *gāyatrī* beginning with *yaṃ dhruva*: "We know that Great Lord, we meditate upon Him who is like lightning in speech; may that Śiva impel us."
Thus has the assembly of mantras been proclaimed for the rite of worshiping Śiva.
Thus concludes the determination of daily rites in the *Tattvaratnāvalī*, a work composed by the venerable teacher Vimalācārya, which is exceedingly pure.
Now I shall describe the occasional [rites]; regarding that, the Sūtra (4b) states:
"Those beginning with Īśāna and those beginning with Hṛdaya have four faces and three eyes."
The four arms are said to hold the spear, the trident, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness;

in some instances, there are eight arms. There are also eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyāpatis), radiant as the directions. Like Brahmā, Īśvara, Guha, and Vaikuṇṭha, there is the quartet beginning with Brāhmī.
The southern [face] is Payasvinī, the eastern is Śūkarāsyā, and the one facing Indra (the north) is considered Dravamatā;
Carcikā, Śūla, Khaṭvāṅga, Kārdvin, Agni, and Tviṭ are the eighth among the Gaṇas.

Having worshipped the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvara), the hosts of attendants (gaṇa), the mothers (mātṛ), and those such as Śāk and Vajra in the world, one should display the ten mudrās; this is the ritual procedure for fulfillment.
For Īśa and the others, the mantras are *surabhi*, the lotus, the trident, and the crocodile;
their seed-syllables and mudrās are those of the heart and other limbs, with the eye-mudrā as the mark in the fire.
The withdrawal of the weapon belongs to the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras); the one called the Lotus belongs to the Gaṇanāthas known as Śūla; and the Bell belongs to the host of Mothers.
The power of the Lord, whose mind's desires are unimpeded, is like a seed that has not yet sprouted; she is the hope for the lineage, tranquil, and arrow-faced.

One should not show the mudrā below; one should lead it toward the upper syllable. Then, with the Śiva-mantra, one should offer incense and a lamp to [the deity] together with his retinue, as well as various kinds of food offerings (naivedya), water for drinking, and water for sipping (ācamanīya).
One should offer to the Great Lord a massage of the hands, betel for the fragrance of the mouth, a mirror, and dūrvā grass, unbroken rice grains, and sacred threads upon his head.
Worship performed without the *pavitra* is declared to be *tāmasī*; for worship performed without it, even if one performs the *paramīkaraṇa*, is *rājasī*.
Whether with one flower, two flowers, three flowers, or eight flowers,
the offering should be performed according to the instructions, the time, and so forth, in accordance with one's age, status, and circumstances.
Having recited [the mantra], one should offer water that has been consecrated by the mantra, wrapped in a protective amulet (*varman*),
guarded by the weapon-mantra (*hetimantra*), and provided with *kuśa* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
6a) With the *udbhavā* mudrā, reciting this while holding the water vessel in his hand:
"O protector of the secret beyond secrets, accept this recitation performed by us."
"Success comes through the object of knowledge when You are present by Your grace.
Thus, one desiring liberation should offer this petition while reciting these two verses.
O God, whatever we do, whether good or evil,
O Śaṅkara, consume that with the syllables *hūṃ* and *kṣa* at the feet of Śiva.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer; Śiva is this entire world.
Everywhere one worships Śiva; I am indeed that very Śiva.

Having recited the mantra ten times the number of limbs [of the deity], and having performed circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise, one should enter within, remain there until the end, and then, being aware [of the time], proceed to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Similarly, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be red, with corners either triangular or circular, or lotus-shaped;
it bestows all desires and is always used for initiations and rites of pacification, measuring one cubit in size.

For fifty [offerings], for one hundred, for a thousand, for ten thousand, for fifty thousand, and for one hundred thousand oblations, the fuel sticks should be measured respectively by a fistful, one finger-breadth, five, ten, twenty-five, and fifty.
In the fifty-lakh [fathom] [measurement], at ten million [fathoms], it reaches the vicinity of Kṛtānta (Yama);
at the measurement of a fist or a cubit, the throat [is measured] by four, four, and six barley-corns respectively.
The neck of others should be increased by one barley-corn for every *hasta* [of height];
in some cases, the girdle and other parts may be increased by half a finger-breadth up to nine fingers.
The two jeweled girdles for a one-cubit [tall] person should be five and a half finger-breadths;
otherwise, for each subsequent size, they increase by two finger-breadths.
In the first triad, it is extended to the navel by fifteen parvas,
and its width is seven and a half parvas at the first joint.
The height [of the first] is seven or eight barley-corns; then the lip is seven or eight barley-corns;
for the remaining seven pits, the height and the horizontal extent [are equal].
Since the yoni increases gradually from two finger-breadths up to three finger-breadths, its height increases by one-fourth;
it is like a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and has corners extending toward the wind (northwest).
6b) In Nirdhāta, [the wheel] has the luster of a lotus; in Vala, it is like a crystal lotus;
in Śīghra, it is like a green lotus; and in Tūrṇa, it belongs to the Lord of Treasures.
The great city of Vīrabhadra is circular, possessing the luster of a white lotus for the Lord of Knowledge (Vidyeśa), the brilliance of a yellow lotus for Śambhu,
and the radiance of a sapphire.
The five groups of eight [sites] are white, red, yellow, and green, shaped like a tortoise with two eyes;
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, and Naimiṣa are located in Puṣkara, which has six faces.
Diṇḍi and Bhārabhūti, Lākulīśa and Guhyamastaka,
Hariścandra and Śrīśaila, as well as Jalmeśa and Āmrātikeśvara.
Mahākāla, Madhyameśa, Kedāra, Abhirava as the eighth,
Gayā, Kurukṣetra, Nākhalā, and likewise Kanakhala.
Vimala, Aṭṭahāsa, Maheṃdra, and Bhīma;
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, and Mahālaya.
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Dvārakṣa, Sthāṇu, Ahama, Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, and Maṇḍaleśvara.
Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthaleśākhya, Sthaleśvara,
and Pañcāntaka— these are situated from Jalādiga to Garvaparvata.
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Pākṣa, Gāndharva, Śākra, Aindra,
Prājāpatya, and Brāhma— this is the ancient classification of marriage forms according to the intellect.
Śoṇāli, Svarṇapīta, Indukuṇḍa, Citrasitaprabha,
Sutaṃda, Karāla, Subhadra, and Surūpavān.
Vibhūti, Asṛta, and Praja are the lords of Brahmā in succession;
[these are] the uncreated (akṛta), the created (kṛta), the worldly (caribhava), the Brāhma, and the infallible (acyuta) within the quality (guṇa).
The youthful [deities] have necks of indescribable form, radiant as the moon;
among men, they are the sole heroes who grant protection with their left hands.
The six cities described before are like variegated tortoises:
Pracaṇḍa, Umādhavaja, Ananta, and Ekaśiva.
7a) Those resembling a red parasol are considered to be in the city of Rāga;
those like crystal parasols are in the cities of Vidyā.
And as before, in the *kalā-tattva*, there are the two cities of Saṃvarta and Jyotiṣ;
in the *niyati* [tattva], the two cities of Śūra and Pañcānta; and in the *kāla* [tattva], the two cities of Hema and Kūrmasviṣ.
O Ekavīraśikha, where are the Śrīkaṇṭhas who abide in reality? There are three worlds resembling tortoises, shining like pure crystal.
O Bhuvaneśa, Mahādeva, Vāmadeva, and Bhavodbhava!
O Ekapiṅga, you who are radiant and the size of a thumb for those who desire the moment.
The perfections of enjoyment and beauty, previously manifested, are wheel-shaped;
in the Vidyā [cakra], they have the luster of five lotuses, and likewise, Hālāhala is in front.
Rudra, Krodha, Aṃvikā, and Ghorā are proclaimed as Vāmadevī;
and Īśvara, Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śiva, and Unmanā are the final ones.
Ekaśaśin, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, and Śikhaṇḍika;
before him is one shaped like a hundred-petaled lotus, endowed with the brilliance of the midday sun.
Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, as well as Śakti and Sadāśiva—
these are the Sarvatobhadra cities within the Sādākhya [tattva], possessing the splendor of ten million moons.
The Śākta [cakra] is radiant like a lotus, and the Śāmbhava is of the same kind;
thus, across all the tattvas, there are one hundred and twenty [cakras].
In this *Bhuvanārcita*, Ananta has been described both briefly and in detail;
furthermore, the intermediate numbers and those situated in the Nairṛta region have also been established.
From Kalā and Agni up to Śiva, there are various colors and forms;
the lords of those worlds, who dwell in their respective cities, possess those same colors.
Accompanied by Rudrāṇī, they possess ten arms;
equal to Sadāśiva, they have dark throats adorned with the crescent moon.
Kālavahni is four-faced Brahmā; those beginning with Brahmā are considered as previously described. Now, the thirty-six principles (tattvas) are explained according to their own essential nature.
Having said "pṛthvī" and "lobhava," one should perform the cooling sprinkling (śītābhīghāraka) with the Saṃhitā mantras joined with *vaṣaṭ* at each repetition, in due order.
Having placed [the deity] upon the sixfold seat in the mandala to the west of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Then, one should perform the purification of the *saṃpāta* [residue] once with the *saṃhitā* [mantra];
having touched the *caru* offering once, one should likewise consume it with the six mantras ending in *pā*.
Having divided [the offering] threefold out of pride,
the wise man should offer two portions mixed with honey and clarified butter to the deity and the sacrificial fire.
Then, having properly colored one's own portion with ghee,
and having bathed the deity with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and other substances, he should offer it.
One should brush the teeth with the *narāśaṃsa* mantra; ashes should be applied to the east and south with the *aghora* mantra, or to the crest-lock on the west with the *śikhā* mantra.
One should touch the *dhātrī* fruit and water with the heart-mantra (*sadyojāta*),
or else with the head-mantra (*vāmadeva*) or the *dhāman*-mantra, when they have been perfumed in the directions.
Water and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) placed within a leaf-cup,
a flower in the direction of Hara (the North), and auspicious yellow pigment (rocanā) in the South-East.
The teacher should be given [an offering] in the southwest, and the fourfold [substance] in the northwest;
one should present the sacrificial materials and *darbha* grass with the *sadyojāta* mantra.
A staff, a rosary, yellow-colored begging bowls,
betel-leaf, saffron, fragrance, and metallic collyrium are pleasing to Rūpin.
The secret keeper should present the voting sticks, a mirror, hair-combing tools,
articles for the use of beautiful women, and other such items.
The sacrificial pap (caru), the lion-throne, the vessel, the sandals, and the headband;
then, for Īśāna, one should offer the thick sacrificial pap with ghee in the Nara [vessel].
What is its own nature? One should conceive of it as being elevated by their minds.
The sacrificial grasses (pavitra), sprinkled with arghya water and consecrated by the recitation of the Saṃhitā mantras,
having been covered with a black antelope skin and other materials, are brought into the presence of the fire.

Remembering Śambhu, whose nature is Time, one should perform the *saṃpāta* rite with the *aṇu-mantras* and the *saṃhitā*, repeating it twenty-one times; then, one should envelop [the disciple] with the armor (*varma*) recited over them.
With a thread, [he should sever] the multitude of causal agents who have taken refuge in vain in the fire of Śiva;
then, having worshipped the Sun and offered perfume and a sacred thread (pavitraka).
Having sipped water (ācamana), one should offer [oblations] to the gatekeepers and to the Lord of the Vidyās;
immediately thereafter, [one offers to] the World-Protectors, the Śiva-pitcher, the Weapon, the Vardhanī vessel, and so forth.
To the feet of Gaṇeśa, Kamalā, and the Lord, and also to one's own self;
then [he offers] that which is called the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitra), having a single knot and consisting of very fine threads.
Having smeared all medicinal herbs and placed them within his joined palms (añjali),
which are filled with flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and dūrvā grass, he should recite the words of invocation.
Oṃ! To you, the Lord who fills all Vedic deficiencies, the true one, I offer this invocation which brings about the attainment of all desires.
Grant success to that sacrifice which is being performed;
O Śambhu, salutations to you in every way and at all times—be gracious to me.
Having thus addressed the God and rendered [the offering] nectar-like through the *recaka* breath,
one should then utter the mantra ending with "Śiva" and request it for the sake of Śiva.
Having completed the recitation of mantras, hymns, and so forth, and having offered the sacrificial oblation (caru) into the Śiva-fire,
one should then bestow the purifying thread (pavitra) upon the Rudra-mantras and others outside [the fire-pit], just as one would for Śiva.
8b) After the Bhūtāditya has offered the bali, there is then the rite for the *pūrṇā* [offering].
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one offers four oblations while circumambulating.
One should unite Śambhu, who resides in the fire, with Śivā, who has been worshipped within the mandala;
having protected the fire within the Vidyā, one should take that [essence] with devotion toward the Guru.
Having placed the sacrificial grass (kaṭa) with weapons laid upon it at the foot of a barren tree and so forth in his mind,
and having established the purifiers (pavitrāṇi) by means of his splendor, his limbs, and the subtle particles of his digits;
Having consecrated it with the Brahma-mantras, one should join it to the heart within the chest;
having covered it with the armor-mantra and bound it with the needle-mantras, one should worship it with the limb-mantras.
Then, having offered [the materials] into the Kumbha-Śambhu and the three fire-mandalas,
one should partake of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the sacrificial porridge (caru), and the tooth-cleansing stick, following the sequence of the [four] wheels.

Having sipped water for purification (ācamana) and performed the ritual of empowering the limbs (sakalīkaraṇa), and having caused the great festival of singing and other arts to be held, one should go to sleep after providing protection while recollecting Śiva.
Then, in the morning, having performed his bath, the twilight prayers, and the libations,
and having taken up the sacred thread (pavitraka) without having formally dismissed it, he [proceeded].
Having placed [the vessel] in a pure bowl within the mandala in the northeast,
the preceptor should dismiss the deity and discard the floral remains (nirmālya) upon the great ground.
Having performed the daily worship, one should then perform the occasional worship toward the Sun,
the lords of the day, the goddesses of fortune, the deities of the site, and the rows of world-protectors.

Having performed the ritual propitiation with mantras and the expiatory rite using the Śara-mantra over the Śiva-pitcher, the weapon-pitcher, the Vardhanī-pitcher, and the fires within the womb of the *lagna*, [one should proceed].
Having offered the sacred thread (pavitra) to Bhānu, and having offered the sacred thread in succession to the door-keepers and others,
one should sit near Śambhu for the recitation of mantras.
In his own form as the Lord of the Gaṇas, Kamalā [is present] at the feet of the Master;
the sacred thread extends from the Śakti-kala up to the body of the Vidyā-kala.
9a) Taking up a purifier (pavitra), one should offer it facing the water jar;
recollecting Śambhu as the embodiment of Time (kālātmaka), one should recite the words of request.
O Lord, by you, whose nature is the syllable *uṃ*, my various states have been experienced:
they were performed, suffered through, abandoned, maintained, concealed, and marveled at.
O Śambhu, by Your will, let all that has been done— whether afflicted or unafflicted, performed or neglected, and whether well-done or ill-done— be rendered pure by this [mind] in its entirety.
Then, one should utter twice the words "pūraya" (fill), followed by the phrase "makha-vrata," then "niyama īśvarāya," ending with "svāhā" and joined with "namaḥ."
Having recited the root mantra ending with *māyā* (HŪṂ), and for the presiding deity of the principle of the self (*ātmatattva*),
one should place the purifying thread upon [the deity] joined with "to Śiva, svāhā" (*śivāya svāhā*).
In this manner, the preceptor, having uttered the principles of Vidya and Shiva,
as well as everything up to Ishvara and up to Shiva, should offer the sacred thread (pavitraka).

Having uttered the root mantra ending with *layāntam*, one should offer the fourth [case-ending] to *sarvatattvādhipāya* (the Lord of all principles) and to *śambhave* (to Śambhu); one who desires worldly enjoyment should begin from Śiva.
Then one should offer the purifying thread (pavitraka) to the faces, the limbs, and the enclosures;
thereafter, one should perform the rites of incense, the waving of lights (ārātrika), the food offering (naivedya), recitation (japa), praise (stuti), and prostration (natikriyā).
Having performed [the rite] for others according to the rule, he should perform it for himself when he is the guest;
and then, like Śiva, he should offer four *pavitrakas* into the fire.
One should offer the inner thread and the purifier (pavitra) to Rudra and the other deities;
then, having clothed the Vidyā and the Guru with devotion, one should present the purifier to them.
Then, having gone into the presence of Śiva and saying "Forgive me," [one should observe] for four,
three, two, or one month, or for a fortnight, or even half of that.

Having undertaken a vow for five days, three days, one day, or until the conclusion of the ritual, according to the Guru’s word and according to his capacity, he should bow down and ask Śiva for forgiveness.
Then, one should give the sacred thread (upavīta) to the ascetics to one another;
having meditated upon the one consisting of Viṣṇu within the portion of nine and seven squares.
9a) Having placed [the fire] in the northeast corner, one should offer oblations with the head for Viṣṇu;
having meditated on one's own body as Raudrī and held it at the navel, one should leap up from that.
Holding a purifier (pavitraka) made of two blades of darbha grass, each a span in length and tied with a knot in the middle,
between the tips of the thumb and the ring finger, one should divide it three times in front of the fire.
Likewise, having performed the leaping with the weapon-mantra and the immersion of the heart, the self,
and the mouth, one should purify [the area] with a firebrand of *darbha* grass burnt by the weapon-mantra.
Having performed the lustration (*nīrājana*) with one [wick] while it is blazing, one should kindle another;
having consumed [the first] with the *astra-mantra*, one should cast the *darbha* grass into the fire.
Having placed a blade of *kuśa* grass with its knot in the middle across the rim, measuring one span (*prādeśa*),
one should fashion one, two, or three channels within the small vessel.
With "Sva" [he offers] into the fire, and with "Ha" into that portion; he should sequentially cast a drop of clarified butter.
From the right with "Dakṣiṇāgnaye Svāhā," and from the left to Soma as before.
At midday, having offered oblations to Agni and Soma,
one should cast the fourth oblation into the manifestation of the eyes and into the mouth, the fire-pan, and so forth.
Oṃ magnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā—thus [it is recited] during the bright fortnight;
however, during the dark fortnight, one should employ Sūrya in the place of Soma.
Having consecrated it with the six-limbed mantra and rendered it immortal by means of the *dhenumudrā*,
one should then veil it with the *kavaca* mantra and protect it with the *heti* mantra.
One should purify even the ghee used for the foot-offerings by offering oblations one by one,
starting from the *ājāti* and ending with the *śapathya*.
Having brought about the striking with the *vaśā* [mudrā], one should then join the curved parts:
the *sadyojāta* with the *guhyaka*, and the *vāmadeva* with the *daruṇa*.
By uttering "Svāhā" to Aghora, Putrasena, Athavara, Mīsa, Sakṛdvratas, Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Nareṣṭa, and Īśa.
Having led [the oblation] from Agni to Vāyu, and having led it to Īśa,
one should effect the unification of the faces with the ladle (sruva) by means of a stream of clarified butter (ājya).
The measurement of the pit (kuṇḍa) is one [unit], while the arrangement of the others is by means of its circumference.
(9a) By performing the fire-oblation (homa) in a pit facing upward, there is liberation; in one facing east, all perfections (siddhis) are attained.
In the southeast, there is the burning of Māra; in the north, peace and good fortune.
In the west, the wise one should perform the daily rites and so forth, offering oblations to his own chosen deity;
thereafter, having performed worship and fire-offerings with the Īśa and Astra mantras.
One should assign names to the fires of the heart: Śivāgni, Svahutāśana, and so forth. Now, the forms and positions of the seven tongues of Agni are described.
HŪṂ Hiraṇyā, drawn by power (vaśa), one should satisfy Vaiśyā in the center;
for paralyzing (staṃbha), LRŪṂ Kanakā in the east; ŚRUṂ Raktā in the southeast for burning (tāpana).
Prūṃ is Kṛṣṇā on the bridge of Tāraṇa; for nourishment, Vrūṃ is Suprabhā in the Supreme;
Prūṃ is Mārutā with a red face; for eradication, she has a smoky form.
In the center is Sūm Vahurūpā, who flows toward the south and north;
she grants all desires, and all [the rivers] possess a luster corresponding to their own names.
It bestows sovereignty, it is swift in burning away [impurities], it brings about death for enemies,
it effects subjugation and eradication, it grants wealth, and it is the giver of liberation.
The tongue that bestows all accomplishments, or else those situated from the east to the center;
having worshipped the two parents of the fire with the heart-mantra, one should dismiss them and complete the rite.
One should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the prescribed rule with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*,
or else with the mantra consisting of the syllables *oṃ āṃ* joined with the fire-seed (*ra*) and the sixteenth vowel (*ī*) along with the nasal bindu (*m*).
By the placement of Paratejīśa, the fire of Śiva arises instantly;
then, within the lotus of the heart, one should [worship] Śiva in the fire according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having performed full worship, one should effect a union between the faces of Īśa and Agni;
having established the connection of the channels (nāḍī-saṃdhāna) by oneself between the sacrificial fire and Śiva.

The wise practitioner, having ascertained the specific sacrificial materials and the required measure of oblations, should perform the fire sacrifice for the limbs with the root mantra at one-tenth the number [of the main sacrifice].

The fire-oblation for a farmer should consist of honey, cow’s milk, and clarified butter; the oblation of curd should be one śukti in measure, while that of the milk-rice preparation (pāyasa) should be one prasṛti.

A third part consists of the roots and all such things beginning with the lotus; this is considered the offering for the festival. Therefore, the powers of Rudra’s mudrās, which destroy obstacles, are now described.
The middle fingers of both hands are bent and made slightly smaller.
In the meantime, when the two index fingers are joined at the hollow of the hand,
with the tips of the thumbs placed upon the root-joints of those [index fingers], this [is the mudrā].
The two little fingers and ring fingers are declared to be "delightful" (manoramā);
having crossed them from one hand to the other, one should then press down with these two.
The remaining [fingers] should be made thick and upward-pointing; this is proclaimed as the *bījamudrā*. A hand with the fingers pressed closely together is proclaimed as the *śaktimudrā*.
The middle fingers of both hands are joined together;
the little fingers and thumbs are positioned above, joined and level like a vajra.
The Praśāntā mudrā is described as follows: with the backs of both hands joined, the fingers are interlaced, and the little fingers are pressed by the thumbs.

When the middle finger is pressed down and the ring finger is raised and joined [with the thumb], this mudrā is called Pañcānana; it is said to be dear to the one born from the sacrificial ladle (Agni).
With the little finger of the lower [hand] placed between those two [other fingers],
the middle fingers of the two hands, being separated, are extended with their tips joined together.
Then, when the two months have elapsed, [the ritual is performed] with the pair of the index finger and the thumb joined together,
through the division of the upward contraction and extension of the *sruk* ladle.

With the two middle fingers joined at the base like a water-pot (*kumbha*) and the two index fingers extended, one forms the *triśūla* (trident) mudrā; the *padma* (lotus) mudrā is like a lotus; the *surabhi* (cow) mudrā has the shape of a cow's udder.
The Liṅgamudrā is proclaimed as being formed by the thumb and the right index finger;
the Kālakarṇī Mahāmudrā is [formed] with the fingers of the left hand facing forward, extending from the tips of the feet up to the head.
It is declared [to be formed] by touching with both hands through the union of the little finger and the thumb.

The extension [of the fingers] from the middle one is called *prasāryata*, while the withdrawal from the little finger is *saṃhṛti*. The branches arise from these two, and their opposites are likewise designated.
With the left hand facing downward, by moving the right hand in a threatening gesture (tarjanī), the two hands—
bent like bells and joined at the wrists— are brought face-to-face with the fingers extended.
Placing the right thumb upon the left thumb and striking with the index fingers,
one should perform the circular threatening gesture of the two hands, pointing the tips of the thumbs and index fingers forward.
The *nimbāmuṣṭi* [mudrā] is formed by the two index fingers and the two middle fingers being widely extended,
while the thumb is moved upward from the palm, like the tips of the curved branches of a bull's horns.
The one named Visphurā, who is free from the dust of passion, resides at the root-joint;
she is considered Jyeṣṭhā, Āvāhā, and Mātā, and is established with her face turned downward.
The *sannidhāna* is considered the invocation when the two fists have their thumbs extended;
those same two [fists], with the thumbs placed inside, are proclaimed as *saṃnirodha*.
The *avaguṇṭhanī* [mudrā] is formed by opening the fist and flickering the index finger;
the *sūkarī* [mudrā] is shaped like a bud through the joining of all five fingers.
The Mudrā known as the Deer is formed by joining the tips of the ring finger and the middle finger;
the Conch Mudrā is an upward-facing fist resembling a conch shell, used for offerings and other rites.
And the designator of the mudrās is "Oṃ Hrīṃ," followed by my name and then "Namaḥ.
Thus ends the determination of occasional rites in the *Tattvaratnāvalī*, a work composed by the illustrious Ācārya Vimala, which is exceedingly pure.
Salutations to that ocean of the nectar of bliss and awakening, wherein the jewel-like world is absorbed and from which the two-fold radiant light shines forth. May my mind be devoted to Him.
Now that initiation has been concluded, the ritual procedure is being explained;
since that [procedure] is preceded by the paths (*adhvan*), the paths are therefore described first.
Mantras, words, and phonemes; worlds, principles, and powers;
and the paths—all these exist as the pervader, having pervaded the mudrās.
10b) That which is called Ajāta, Vāma, and Aghora is the head, the heart, and the torso in the Puruṣa;
the Śikhā and Caryā are the root of the vision, and these are proclaimed as the mantras of the body.
In some traditions, it is held that the heart, head, crest, armor, and the root mantra constitute the limbs;
herein lie the eighty-one words of the great mantra Vyomavyāpin.
The paths of the feet are hidden somewhere; there are also the ninefold words.

To the one who pervades the sky, to the one whose form is space, to the all-pervading Śiva, to the infinite, to the unoriginated, to the unsupported, to the fixed, to the eternal, to the one established on the seat of yoga, to the eternally united.

For the sustenance of meditation: Oṃ, salutations to Śiva! To Śiva, the source of all; to the one whose head is Īśāna; to the one whose face is Tatpuruṣa; to the one whose heart is Aghora; to the one whose secret organ is Vāmadeva; to the one whose form is Sadyojāta; to the one who delights in vows, the most secret of secrets; to the one whose end is in the sky; to the sovereign lord of all vidyās.

To the Lord of all sciences; to the one whose form is light; to the one who is beyond the Supreme Lord; to the conscious-unconscious; to the sky (vyomin) twice; to the pervasive (vyāpin) twice; to the pervasive (*); to the formless (adrūpa) twice; to the primordial (prathama) twice; to the brilliance (tejas) twice; to the light (jyotis) twice; to the formless; to the non-fire; to the smokeless; to the waterless; to the beginningless; to the sound (nā) thrice; to the wind (dhū) thrice. Oṃ bhūḥ. Oṃ bhuvaḥ. Oṃ.

By means of the syllables situated on the petals from the center to the northeast, each one in turn occupying the center,
one should form the eighty-one-fold grid (ekāśītipada) through the manifestation within the central square.

In some places there are exactly five words, led by the letter *a* and the nasal bindu; here, the phonemes are considered to begin with *a* and end with *kṣa*, while in other cases they are held to begin with *ka* and end with *a*.

The mantras, words, and syllables shine forth, radiant with streaming rays of light.

Although the worlds are innumerable, those that are principal therein will be described briefly, in their proper order beginning with Kāla-vahni, for the sake of accomplishing the ritual procedure (vidhi).
The city of Kālāgni is a blazing triangle, while that of Kuṣmāṇḍa is likewise;
the city of Hāṭakeśa has the appearance of an umbrella and is brilliantly illuminated by various jewels.
The Brahmā-maṇḍala of Viṣṇu is like a ruby lotus; that of Rudra is like a blue lotus;
and the Sārvato-bhadra is like the fierce sun, established upon the ground.
The [lineage] of Ananta originates from the blue lotus; that of the Skull-bearer (Kapālin) has the luster of a golden lotus;
and that of Vahni resembles a red lotus—each being firm and well-proportioned.
11b) It should always be free from hair and the like, knotted, and made very beautiful; the thread, having been washed by one who is pure, should then be purified by means of silver.
Having understood the perfection of the thread, one should tie it with the Vāmadeva mantra.
Or, by means of threads of the reality of syllables, phonemes, and kalās, one may perform the purification.
The twelve-fingered *vāśigamānaka* should be made entirely like the *mauli*, with all its knots and internal spaces complete.
Ten knots should be made, or else that [number] according to the sequence:
Oṃkāra, Śarābhṛt, Vahni,
Svabhū, Gāga, Yu, Hau, Prakṛti, Pauruṣī, Vīryā, and the fourth shall be Aparājitā.
Jayā, Vijayā, likewise Ajitā,
Sadāśivā, Mano— [the eighth], and the ninth is Sarvajñā, while the tenth is Ājñā.
Those known as the "Lotus of the Text" (Granthapadma) are equal in splendor to the sun;
they reside upon altars made of jewels, stone, wood, or clay, or in self-arisen [images].
One should offer a single *kārpa* measure of purified substances along the path according to one's inclination,
like Śiva, within the fires situated in the regions prescribed by the *sūtras*.
One should provide a purifying thread (*pavitraka*) for each of those individually in another manner:

one for one's own form, for the limbs, for the weapons, for the feet, and likewise for the staff; similarly, one for each [of the deities] at the doors, for the guardians of the directions, for the water-jars (*kalaśa*), and so forth.

In the case of the *liṅga* as well, it is always desired that there be more [of them]; even in a single place, there may be nine or more, starting from nine up to twelve, with an increase of one for each.
From twenty-eight, by increasing the number of rows, one reaches one hundred and eight;
from that thread of one hundred and eight, there is one [thread] less, namely ninety-seven.

In the *Kājuṣa*, it is stated that from the *piṇḍikā* upwards, there is no beauty beyond eighteen fingers; however, in the *Gaṅgādharatāraka*, there is a rule regarding knots (*granthi*) for the *karmasādi* [and other] types, based on an increase of two knots starting from the third and eighteenth [fingers].

12a) For moving, stationary, desired, or manifest [objects], one should touch up to the knees; for a bull, one should likewise touch its horns, back, hump, neck, and hooves, as it is sacred to all the gods.
One should conquer the ninth obstacle with red sandalwood, saffron from Kashmir, musk, yellow pigment, indra-tree resin, turmeric, red ochre, and so forth.
When people are asleep, for three months during both the bright and dark fortnights,
one should perform the *dhivāsa* (preliminary consecration) on the day of the *smara* (the twelfth lunar day), provided it falls on a Sunday.
Having worshipped the Destroyer of Sacrifice (Śiva) with garments, ornaments, and garlands,
and having performed the ritual bathing for the occasion, as well as the twilight prayers and libations, he engaged in his religious duties.
Having worshipped the Sun upon the prepared seat, beginning with the worship of the doors and so forth,
one should perform the rite of satiating the mantras according to the procedure to be described hereafter.
Then, [place] the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (carusthālī), which has been washed with weapons, wrapped in cloth,
and whose neck is encircled by a wick made of excellent cotton over which armor-mantras have been recited.
Having placed [the image] anointed with sandalwood and other unguents within the mandala of the six seats, one should worship Śiva there with offerings of meditative visualization.
Or, one may worship with external perfumes and other offerings a [liṅga] whose face is covered by a cloth;
when it has been purified through initiation and other rites, one should likewise face the same direction as the [liṅga’s] front.
When [the vessel] has been placed to the right of the fire-pit, its seed-syllable of egoity having been dispersed,
one should place the cooking pot upon it, which has been cleansed with ghee from a cow consecrated by the weapon-mantra.
One should purify the vessel with the Astra-mantra and consecrate it one hundred times with the Mūla-mantra;
it should be joined with four handfuls (prasṛti) of sacrificial rice.
In the ritual procedure for initiation, for the sake of the disciple, one should gradually increase the *prasṛti* measure;
one should cook the *caru* oblation in the fire of Śiva while reciting the root mantra.
While stirring it with the mantra, one should protect it with the armor-mantra (kavaca).
If the sacrificial porridge (caru) does not boil, disease will arise; if it burns, death will follow from that.
Once it is well-cooked, having offered the *samhitā* mantras and the heated *abhighāraka* libation,
one should remove the vessel and place it upon a *maṇḍala* of *darbha* grass consecrated with the *astramantra*.
One should drive away the obstacle with the *dhruva* mantra and pierce the heart with the *hṛdaya* mantra.
For householders,
such as the twice-born and others, there are six, two, one, and one [verses] respectively.
Having offered the deficient oblations for the purpose of removing defects, and having presented the final full oblation;
Having dismissed Śiva who resides within the fire and offered oblations with the Vyāhṛtis, he then [performed] the rites for the fire,
the sun, and so forth.
Then he should offer the purifying oblation (pavitra) and present the sacrificial offering (bali) to the guardians of the directions outside;
he should feed the Liṅgins, the learned, and also the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
Having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's capacity on the path of power (*śakti*), one should perform the rites and so forth through this gift, O Saṃkara.
Having performed the morning bath and other rites, one should bring the sacred threads for the Lord;
having worshipped the God with the eightfold flowers, one should perform the ritual dismissal.
Having performed the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika),
and [other] rites, and having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the mantra for atonement (prāyaścitta),
one who desires liberation should perform the dedication of the ritual action to Bharga.
By your grace,
having placed the multitude of mantras— which accomplish the fruit— within the heart, one should dismiss the Śiva-fire.
Having joined the Valimantras and the gaze with [the deity] in Śivā, saying "forgive me" while still requiring [her presence], one should dismiss her;
one should dismiss the Door-deities, Vastu, Gaṇas, and World-protectors without further requirement.
Then, having worshipped Candra and offered him the *pavitraka*,
one should give [the offering] to the Guru with devotion.
Therefore, O Lord Caṇḍanātha, by your command, may my limbs now be made complete.
Having thus made this request, bowed down, offered praise, and presented the valuable offerings,
one should cast the floral remains (*nirmālya*) and other such items into the waters of the well of existence (*bhava*).
13a) Having purified the ground and bathed the Lord of Gods, one should worship Him;
at the conclusion, one should offer the vow and feed [the preceptor] according to the Lord of Yoga.
The procedure for the tenth festival day is likewise prescribed;

O you who are far-sighted, like a vessel for this [sacrificial] rite, come hither!

Having first invoked Pavana and the rest,

The root, the stalk, the leafless branch, the flower, and the fruit in succession, along with soft earth,
cow dung, ash, a tooth-stick, and fragrant substances— these are [the materials].
One should place [the mantras] beginning with *ajānāt* and *hṛdā* in the west and other directions;
then, one should consecrate the five limbs in the hollowed palms (*añjali*) with the blazing mantra of Śiva.
O Lord of Gods, O Master, you were invited by me this morning;
since the Dāmana festival is being performed on the mountain, please remain present here.
Having recited the root mantra of the deity and offered a handful of flowers with joined palms,
one should place the remainder in that vessel according to the ritual procedure for the *pavitraka*.
In the morning, one should perform the ritual worship with unbroken *damana* sprouts.
Taking a water-pot joined with dūrvā grass and other items,

and [offering] with the three principles (*tritatva*) and the *śaṃvara* mantras, one should perform the filling of the vessel for the Lord of the Sky (*kheśvara*), offering the root-mantra (*mūla*) and the sacrifice (*makha*) with the words "to the Lord of the Sky. One should perform the rite of fulfillment.
One should offer [the oblation] with this mantra, beginning with "Bhava" and joined with "Namaḥ" at the end of the fourth case for Sūlapāṇi; the remainder should be performed as previously described.
The Guru is situated upon the chest of the Vedas, which are like a mountain.
13b) The mind is like half-sleep; it abides upon the sevenfold lotus-seat,
red in color, triangular, and possessing the characteristic mark of its own fire-element.
The Vāyu-tattva is black and circular, sealed and conjoined;
the Gandha-tanmātra has the luster of gold, and its taste is like that of clarified butter;
its form is like the Japā flower, and its touch is rough.
The subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra) is the cloud, the generative organ (upastha), and has a green luster; the foot is yellow, the hand is white,
and the discus is likewise.
In some places, there is a white covering of such a form;
the nose has the luster of molten gold, and the tongue has a radiance equal to the moon.
Likewise, one should visualize Kṛṣṇa, who is as black as collyrium; this is the fivefold manifestation of that which has become the earth-element.
It was taken away;
that pride of the enjoyment of smoke and fire, resembling a lotus with its stalk uprooted, was destroyed; the lotus-bed was laid low, and the sun rose like a newly emerged day-maker.
That [nature] consists of the qualities (guṇas).
The male [deity], radiant with protection, and the Rāghu-vidyā, red in hue, emerged from the mouth of the Śivā. The Kalā, resembling a red lotus, and Niyati... Kāla, black as a blue lotus...
The reality of the Lord...
resembling ten million moons, known as Bhadra, blazing with light,
[resembling] ten million rising suns, [possessing] a body that is radiant and trembling.
And the presiding deities of the principles, beginning with earth and ending with Śiva, are drawn forth.
Śarva, Paśupati, Īśa, Bhīma, and Prajāpati.
14a) Fire, the earth, Varuṇa,
the sun, wind, the deities of the directions, the moon, Rudra, Brahmā, and Gaṇeśa.
Śrīkaṇṭha, Manmatha, Krodha, Saṃvarta, the one known as Sūra,
Ekavīra, Ananta, Śuddhavidyā, and Sadāśiva.
And because they reside within the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī), these are considered the presiding deities of the principles (tattva):
the thirty-four consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*, together with the fourth and first vowels.
All thirty-six principles (tattvas), beginning with Earth and ending with Primordial Matter (prakṛti), are endowed with Bindu and Nāda; the syllable *ku* is considered their designator.
In the Pauruṣa Tantra, the letter *ka* is remembered as being in the fourfold set beginning with passion (*rāga*);
*laḥ-kṛti-namaḥ* is remembered in the Vidyā; and *kṣaḥ* is remembered as the mantra in the Nava-vidyā.
Ra and Īśa are always auspicious; Śak and Śabha are auspicious in some cases.
The square of the Self-principle (Ātmatattva) is red, and its presiding deity is Brahmā.
The Vidyātattva is golden-hued, possesses sixty-four [deities], has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity,
is pure like crystal, is circular in shape, and has Sāndhya as its presiding deity.
The principle of the Self (ātmatattva) is sometimes considered to have four faces and yellow arms; the principle of Ignorance (avidyātattva) is proclaimed as gentle, blue, and possessing eight arms.

The mantra for the Śiva-tattva is: *Śivatatva-śaśāṅkāntaṃ pañcavaktraṃ caturbhujaṃ sabindudīrghanitayaṃ kramāt tattvādyaṃ manuḥ*. (The mantra begins with the word "Śivatatva," followed by the moon [the letter 'i'], the five faces [the letter 'u'], the four arms [the letter 'e'], the bindu, and the three long vowels [ā, ī, ū] in sequence.)
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Śāntyatītā—
these five are declared to be the powers (śaktis) of Śiva, known as the Kalās.
Her form consists of the five elements, or she may be represented individually;
holding a rosary in her right hand and a lotus with the gesture of fearlessness in her left.
Adorned with all ornaments and possessing three eyes, she is proclaimed as Vivṛtti;
[she arises] from the white [syllable], consisting of two petals...
(15a) Holding a rosary in her right hand and a noose and a lotus in her left, she is fearful.
This Pratiṣṭhā is proclaimed as adorned with all ornaments;
she has three eyes, five faces, is red in color, possesses three umbrellas, and has four arms upon a lotus.
Holding a rosary in her right hand and the Vidyā in her left, she bears a lotus and the Śakti;
adorned with matted hair, a digit of the moon, and ornaments, she possesses the luster of fire.
Seated upon a six-petalled lotus, she is smoke-colored, four-armed, and has the face of an arrow;
she holds a rosary and the gesture of granting fearlessness in her right hands, and a lotus and a banner in her left.
The three-eyed one wearing a serpent as a sacred thread is said to be the powerful Śānti;
she is seated upon a lotus on a corpse, possessing three eyes, five faces, and four arms.
Holding a rosary in her right hand and the goddess Sarasvatī in her left,
she resembles a jewel of universal form and is proclaimed as Śāntyatītā (Beyond Peace).
In some places, all [the deities] have five faces, ten arms, and three eyes;
the mantras of the Kalās are *hlāṃ*, *hkīṃ*, *hrūṃ*, *hyai*, *hrauṃ*. Now, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is described.
In the Nivṛtti[-kalā], the reality is the Pārthiva-tattva, accompanied by sixteen puruṣas;
there is one vowel and twenty-eight syllables in reverse order.
The two Śaṃvaras are born from the heart; the two seed-syllables are considered to be the letters A and LAUM.
The two channels are known as Īḍā and Piṅgā, and the two winds are Prāṇa and Apāna.
The vital breath and the organ of generation; the object of smell; the pentad of qualities;
the state known as Sarvatobhadra; and the cause, which is the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā).
The *Pratiṣṭhā*, *Avadāna*, and others, along with the castes (*varṇas*) and the wings of qualities (*guṇapakṣatis*), constitute fifty-six *pura*s; here, there are twenty-one *padā*s.
The head and the two left [channels] are said by Manu to be the two seeds beginning with *nu* and *va*;
the *nāḍī* [is] Suṣumnā, and the two [channels] Gāndhārī and Kā are Udāna and Samāna.
Mukunda [is characterized by] the four qualities of the void, air, fire, and water,
as well as the state of dreaming.
16a) One who possesses right mindfulness.
The Guru, having summoned the disciple and being joined with the meditation on Śiva,
should provide the tooth-stick in the place designated for the bound soul (paśu) after the disciple has sipped water (ācānta).
A tooth-stick produced from a milk-tree, twelve finger-breadths in length and highly recommended,
should be touched with water by means of the heart-mantra, the mantra with its limbs, or the radiant mantra.
Having washed the head and face, one should then raise the fall [of the body] from that point;
facing east, north, west, or upward, this downward fall is the most excellent.

Then, having had the disciple perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and having consecrated his body with the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite, he should lay him down in a pure place while muttering the *svapnamāṇavaka* mantra.
Then, having risen at dawn, the Guru should reflect upon the dream;
if the dreams are auspicious, he should delay, but if they are auspicious, he should commence the initiation.
Now, regarding the procedure for initiation: there, having performed the daily obligatory rites and having offered the *arghya*, the preceptor should worship at the door and in the pavilion.
Having entered the inner sanctum according to the prescribed rite and having assumed an internal countenance,
one should perform the purification of the body for the sake of the inner sacrifice, the water offering (argha), and worship.
The purification of the ritual materials, the tilaka, the worship of one's own seat and of oneself,
then the purification of the mantra, followed by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and then the scattering of the vikirā offerings.
The knower of mantras should fashion the sword of knowledge from the seven [syllables] consecrated with mantra;
then, according to the sequence of Śiva’s emanation, he should purify the path that is partless (niṣkala).
One should install the white Uṣṇīṣa mantra recited over the root-mantra, as well as the Karaṅka and Kārā mantras;
then, having prepared the Hand of Śiva, one should be endowed with the Sword of Knowledge.
Identifying with "I am Śiva," established in the fivefold authority,
one should perform the consecration of the pavilion while facing the northeast, starting from the southwest.
Immediately thereafter, one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water from the arghya vessel;
then, having purified it through the rites ending at the crossroads, such as the ritual inspection (vīkṣaṇa) and others.
One should scatter the offerings there and gather them together with a blade of *kuśa* grass;
having worshipped the deities of the site within a mandala established in the southwest (nairṛta).
One should worship Lakṣmī at the western gate, raining down a flood of jewels;
[one should worship her] in the northeast, situated amidst all kinds of grain, in a vessel filled with water scented with jewels.

Having worshipped Śambhu upon the seat of *valā* in the pitcher adorned with cloth and other ornaments, one should worship the *vardhanī* vessel on its right side upon the seat of scattered offerings (*vikira*).
One should worship the lords of the directions, beginning with Śakra and ending with Viṣṇu, in their respective quarters according to the prescribed rite;
one should then cause the *vardhanī* vessel to be carried in front, pouring a stream of water while circumambulating clockwise.
Then, with a *śiva-kuṃbha* (auspicious water-pot) upon his back, he should proclaim the command of Śiva:
"O Śakra and the other gods, for the sake of pacifying obstacles in your respective directions!"
One must remain vigilant until the end of the sacrifice by the command of Śiva.
First, one should place the *kumbha* (vessel) upon one's own seat, and thereafter the *vardhanī*.
Having worshipped Śambhu seated on a firm throne within the pitcher (kumbha), one should place there the path attained;
and having honored the auspicious one seated upon the Vardhanī, who is situated upon a lion and possesses the splendor of the sun at the time of universal dissolution.
One should perform the reconnection of those two with the mudrā known as āliṅga;
one should touch the *kumbha* with the thumb, and the *vardhanī* with the fist at the heart.
For the sake of enjoyment and liberation, one should first touch the *vardhanī* vessel with the fist;
having recited the mantras, one should offer the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*) for the protection of the altar.
Having worshipped Vighnanātha in the northwest for the pacification of obstacles,
one should worship Sthāṇḍileśa in the center upon a maṇḍala prepared with perfumes and other offerings.
Having performed the placement of the path to be purified, one should approach the vicinity of the fire-pit;
having placed the sacrificial fuel, darbha grass, sesame seeds, and so forth on the southern side.
Then, having placed the perfumes, clarified butter, the water-offering (argha), and so forth on the left,
one should consecrate the fire in the sacrificial pit with the *saṃjyā* and other rites, and worship Śiva within that fire.
17a) Having assigned the two paths [of time and space], the Guru should establish the primacy of the face of the Lord [Śiva];
having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra, and a tenth part with the limb-mantras.
Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should likewise sacrifice a hundred oblations for the entry of the disciple;
a hundred and a hundred should be offered when the place and time are propitious.
Likewise, for the sake of neutralizing bad omens and establishing good omens,
one should perform the propitiation of the mantras by offering oblations once.
The consecration is performed with mantras encapsulated by the syllable *hūṃ* and ending in *huṃ phaṭ*;
having prepared the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and offered a portion of it to Śiva and Agni.
After offering a hundred oblations with the Astra-mantra, the wise one then offered an internal sacrifice;
having thus petitioned Maheśa and received his permission, the younger brother went outside.
On a mandala formed by minute particles of weapons upon excellent darbha grass with their tips pointing eastward,
he should place the disciple, whose body is upright, upon a single lotus of life-force.
The preceptor should perform the ablution with four water-pots covered with cloth and sandalwood paste;
for the sake of attaining prosperity and success, he should offer oblations toward the northeast.
One should gaze at the tip of the nose for the sake of enjoyment, or otherwise for the sake of liberation,
with the eyes fixed upon the root-mantra while emitting the Śiva-energy.
Having sprinkled [the site] with water empowered by the Astra-mantra, one should strike it with ashes;
then, having sprinkled it again with Astra-water, one should scratch [the ground] with the tips and roots of Darbha grass.
One should place [the elements] threefold, above the navel for enjoyment and below for liberation; by the reverse order, one should worship Śiva as the self of the mantra upon the head of that body.
And having performed the placement of the path to be purified, one should [purify] the eyes with the *netra* [mantra] and the heart with the *hṛd* [mantra],
using either white [sindūra] that has not been employed, or another [substance] together with its location.
Having covered it and entered within the southern mandala of Śiva.
Then, having seated the disciple in the Ṣaducchāsanaka [posture], the Guru [should dissolve] himself into the disciple's heart by means of the Saṃhāra-mudrā and the Mūrti-mantra.
Having restrained the breath and purified the body, and having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*),
one should worship Śambhu along with his limbs in the hand, and then [worship him] on the head with the root mantra.
Having placed [the mind] there, one should meditate with the radiance of mantras upon that which is free from blemish;
by the yogi who has reached the end of *bindu* and *nāda*, the state of Rudreśvara is attained.
Then, having placed a flower upon that cloth, he should cast it into Śivā;
thereafter, having unveiled the eyes, he should show the Lord of Devas, who bestows both liberation and worldly enjoyment.

According to the falling of the flower, the Guru should assign the names Śiva, Deva, or Aṅgaṇā; or else, he may do so for the Brahmins and others in their respective order, or according to his own will.
Having bowed to the Śiva-pitcher (kuṃbha), the weapon-vessel (astra), and the vardhanī near the fire,
he should seat the disciple on his own southern seat, facing north.
With its tip resting on the master’s shanks and its root grasped by the base of the *kuśa* grass,
that channel, under the guise of the *kuśa*, has entered the abode of the master’s channel.
Having gone to the disciple’s heart by means of the *recaka* breath with the *śiva-āṇu* mantra,
and having returned to one's own heart-lotus by means of the *pūraka* breath.
Desiring [this], one should perform the conjunction of the channels with oneself by means of the auspicious fire;
thereafter, for the sake of that purpose, one should offer three oblations from the root.
One should perform the *saṃpāta* (pouring of remnants) upon the head of the best disciple with the *saṃhitā-mantras*.
For the sake of stabilizing the *śivahasta*, one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
Then one should give the sacred thread (upavīta), consecrated with the root mantra;
by this, one who desires [initiation] shall become fit through the common initiation (*sāmānyadīkṣā*).
